catalog_quote: 1.4 STRESS. Contrastive primary word stress /´/ has been noted falling on the ultimate and penultimate syllables: baháw 'leftover food' and báhaw 'to be healed', toqód 'tree stump' and tóqod 'purpose', sabét 'to understand' and sábet 'to discuss'. Primary word stress on the penultimate syllable of a reduplicated root denotes that the reduplication involves a single stress group rather than two stress groups. Secondary word stress then falls on the syllable preceding the syllable with the primary stress. ... 1.5 PRACTICAL ORTHOGRAPHY ... (2) Primary word stress will not be written on the penultimate syllable. It will be written as acute accent on the ultima and as a circumflex when the stress symbol and grave accent occur over the same vowel: /baráto/ barato 'cheap', /sabét/ sabét 'understand', and /sapáq/ sapâ 'water'.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Rendered PDF page 27 of book p. 25, running head 'PHONOLOGY 25') and page 4 of at 150 and 300 dpi and read the page images. Section 1.4 STRESS reads exactly as quoted: 'Contrastive primary word stress /'/ has been noted falling on the ultimate and penultimate syllables: bahaw [acute on -haw] "leftover food" and bahaw [acute on ba-] "to be healed", toqod [acute on -qod] "tree stump" and toqod [acute on to-] "purpose", sabet [acute on -bet] "to understand" and sabet [acute on sa-] "to discuss".' followed by the reduplication paragraph verbatim; section 1.5 (2) reads 'Primary word stress will not be written on the penultimate syllable. It will be written as acute accent on the ultima and as a…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Mamanwa has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this is the first placement statement held by the project: contrastive final vs penultimate stress, penult unmarked in the orthography, plus a secondary-stress rule for reduplicated roots. It is compatible with the (empty) record and supplies its content.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is phonemic (contrastive) and falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable; minimal pairs are given for both positions. The practical orthography leaves penultimate stress unwritten and marks only final stress (acute, or circumflex when it coincides with a final glottal stop), which treats the penult as the default position and the ultima as the marked one.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In a reduplicated root that forms a single stress group with primary stress on the penult, secondary stress falls on the syllable immediately preceding the primary-stressed syllable (e.g. nakapanáwpanaw 'able to walk about a little', banígbanig 'small mat').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the reduplication pattern. The morphophonemic alternation section (pp. 61-64) treats only segmental changes (vowel harmony of -en/-on, syncope, metathesis) and says nothing about stress shift under suffixation.
new_statements.identity_note: Miller & Miller 1976 is based on the authors' residence in Sitio Pangaylan, Santiago, Agusan del Norte, 1957-1975 (Introduction 0.1, p. 16); section 0.3 Dialect notes (p. 17) says the Mamanwa area 'appears to be dialectally fairly homogeneous with slight intonation or vocabulary differences', and singles out only Zezeqan (Walat), spoken in Bacuag and north of Lake Mainit, as a divergent variety. The stress statement is thus for the Pangaylan (Agusan del Norte) variety.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim with diacritics on p. 25 of the held Miller & Miller 1976 phonology chapter (Rosetta excerpt) and on the same page of the full SIL scan we hold; the held 1991 Mamanwa Texts Appendix A independently restates 'Word stress is also phonemic'. The deciding source is the standard (and only) reference grammar by the principal fieldworkers. Searches of Glottolog's list, the SIL archive language page, Crossref, ScholarSpace (Lobel 2013) and the SEAlang Zorc archive turned up no later phonology, prosody or instrumental study of Mamanwa; the three open items downloaded (Zorc notes, Lobel 2013, Miller 1969) are silent on stress and none contradicts lexical (penult ~ final contrast). Only gap: the Millers' own 1964 PSSHR phonemics article, print-only, which would at most refine the descriptive rule. Coding lexical, right-edge two-syllable window, stands; no action needed.

sources.quote: No statement on Mamanwa stress. Mamanwa forms are cited with accent marks on varying syllables (haó, kanáo, paníi, ijá, duró vs. karíni, ngaríni), consistent with lexical accent but not discussed; the general remark that 'most languages native to Mindanao ... have lost contrastive stress' (p. 287 fn. 3) does not name Mamanwa.
